A statistical research question can be formulated as "Is $Y$ explained by $X$?" or "Does $Y$ depend on $X$?" In this kind of question, $Y$ is referred to as the **response variable**, and $X$ is referred to as the **explanatory variable**. The two-sample t-test addresses this kind of question when $Y$ is numeric (following a normal distribution) and $X$ is categorical with two levels. The ANOVA is when $Y$ is numeric and $X$ is categorical with three or more levels. In this chapter, both $X$ and $Y$ are numeric, and we assume that the expectation of $Y$ changes with respect to $X$.

## Case Study 1: Height and Weight of NBA Players

The research question is whether the expected weight increases with respect to height or not among basketball players. The dataset $\texttt{chicago-bulls-1996-97.csv}$ is the roster of $n = 15$ players of Chicago Bulls in the season of 1996-97.

```{r}
#| label: read-bulls
bulls <- read_csv("data/chicago-bulls-1996-97.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) ### read data
head(bulls) # print rows
```

The column $\texttt{Wt}$ is the body weight in pounds, and the column $\texttt{Ht}$ is the height in inches. As our objective is to explain the weight ($\texttt{Wt}$) by the height ($\texttt{Ht}$), the weight is the response variable, and the height is the explanatory variable in our analysis. The two numeric variables can be visualized using the **scatterplot**. Can we see any linear pattern in the random data points?

```{r}
#| label: bulls-scatterplot
gf_point( Wt ~ Ht, data = bulls,
      title = "Chicago Bulls Players in 1996-97",
      xlab = "Height (inches)",
      ylab = "Weight (pounds)" ) |> 
  gf_lm()
```

## Sample Covariance

In this section, we quantify the direction and strength of linear relationship between two numeric variables. Let $(X_i, Y_i)$ be the paired variables of the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ subject in a sample for $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$. The **sample covariance** is a statistic which is defined as follows:

$$
S_{XY} = \frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})
$$ {#eq-cov}

where $\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ and $\bar{Y} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$ are the sample means. The sample covariance measures the average deviation of each variable from the mean. If $Y_i$ is expected to be above $\bar{Y}$ when $X_i$ is above $\bar{X}$, the sample covariance is positive. If $Y_i$ is expected to be above $\bar{Y}$ when $X_i$ is below $\bar{X}$, the sample covariance is negative. Below is the calculation of sample covariance of $\texttt{Ht}$ and $\texttt{Wt}$.

```{r}
#| label: bulls-covariance

bulls_cov <- bulls |> 
  select(Player, Position, Ht, Wt) |> 
  mutate(mean_ht = mean(~Ht),
         mean_wt = mean(~Wt),
         dev_ht = Ht - mean_ht,
         dev_wt = Wt - mean_wt,
         dev_ht_wt = dev_ht*dev_wt)
bulls_cov


bulls_cov |> 
  summarize(covariance = sum(dev_ht_wt/(n()-1)))

```

The calculated sample covariance of $\texttt{Ht}$ and $\texttt{Wt}$ is $+66.5$. Its unit is inches $\times$ pound, and it is not easy to be interpreted in the context. At least, its sign ($+$) indicates that the player's weight is expected to be above the average weight (219 pounds) when the player's height is above average (80 inches). The sample covariance can be simply calculated by the $\texttt{cov}$ function.

```{r}
#| label: bull-cov-r
cov( Wt ~ Ht, data = bulls ) ### sample covariance of height and weight
```

## Sample Correlation

The **sample correlation** is defined as

$$
R_{XY} = \frac{S_{XY}}{S_{X} \, S_Y}
$$

where $S_{XY}$ is the sample covariance defined in @eq-cov and

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_X & = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2 } \, , \\
S_Y & = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2 }
\end{aligned}
$$

are the sample standard deviations of each variable. Continuing from the calculation of sample covariance of $\texttt{Ht}$ and $\texttt{Wt}$, below is the calculation of sample correlation of $\texttt{Ht}$ and $\texttt{Wt}$.

```{r}
#| label: cor-cov
bulls_cov |> 
  summarize(covariance = sum(dev_ht_wt/(n()-1)),
            correlation = covariance/(sd(~Ht)*sd(~Wt)))
```

Alternatively, the sample correlation can be calculated by the $\texttt{cor}$ function.

```{r}
#| label: cor-bulls
cor( Wt ~ Ht, data = bulls ) ### sample correlation of height and weight
```

The sample correlation 0.719 is a unitless statistic, so it does not have a clear interpretation. Instead, we verbally describe the sample correlation as in Table @tbl-cor. (The verbal description varies by research areas, textbooks, literature, etc.) According to @tbl-cor, the height and weight of Chicago Bulls players have a very strong positive correlation.

| Range          | Description                   |
|----------------|-------------------------------|
| $(+0.7, +1)$   | Strong positive correlation   |
| $(+0.3, +0.7)$ | Moderate positive correlation |
| $(+0.1, +0.3)$ | Weak positive correlation     |
| $(-0.1, +0.1)$ | Negligible correlation        |
| $(-0.3, -0.1)$ | Weak negative correlation     |
| $(-0.7, -0.3)$ | Moderate negative correlation |
| $(-1, -0.7)$   | Strong negative correlation   |

: Verbal description of sample correlation

## Case Study 2: Units and Study Hours

The dataset $\texttt{studyhours.csv}$ is a sample of $n = 110$ college students in an introductory statistics course. The column $\texttt{units}$ is the number of units taking in the semester, $\texttt{hours}$ is the study hours per week outside of classroom, and both $\texttt{units}$ and $\texttt{hour}$ are numeric variables. Can study hours be explained by units?

```{r}
#| label: study-hours-data
studyhours <- read_csv("data/studyhours.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: study-hours-plot
gf_point(hours ~ units, data = studyhours,
      title = "Students in Introductory Statistics Course",
      xlab = "Semester units",
      ylab = "Study hours per week" ) |> 
  gf_lm()
```

```{r}
#| label: corr-study-hours
cor( hours ~ units, data = studyhours ) ### sample correlation of units and study hours
```

Interpret the sample correlation for units and hours studied.







## Properties of Sample Correlation

The sample correlation is a universal statistic for quantifying the direction and strength of the linear relationship between two numeric variables $X$ and $Y$. It has the following properties:

1.  The sample correlation is a unitless statistic.
2.  The sample correlation is between –1 and +1. (They imply a perfect negative and positive linear relationship, respectively.)
3.  The sample correlation of $X$ and $Y$ is the same as the sample correlation of $Y$ and $X$.
4.  A sample correlation of zero implies that no linear relationship is observed between $X$ and $Y$.
5.  It measures a linear relationship only, and does not measure a non-linear relationship.

Below are scatterplots of hypothetical samples and their sample correlations.

```{r}
#| label: corr-examples
#| echo: false
library(patchwork)

N <- 10000

set.seed(123)
x <- rnorm(N)

set.seed(1243)
y_pos_075 <- 0.75 * x + rnorm(N)

set.seed(12434)
y_pos_025 <- 0.25 * x + rnorm(N)

set.seed(12)
y_zero <- rnorm(N)

y_neg_1 <- -x

set.seed(1243)
y_neg_075 <- -0.75 * x + rnorm(N)

set.seed(1243)
y_neg_025 <- -0.25 * x + rnorm(N)

set.seed(12345678)
y_squared <- x^2 + rnorm(N, mean = 0.5)

plot_data <- list(
  list(y = x,        label = "1",      ylim = c(-10, 10)),
  list(y = y_pos_075, label = "0.6",    ylim = c(-10, 10)),
  list(y = y_pos_025, label = "0.25",   ylim = c(-10, 10)),
  list(y = y_zero,    label = "0",      ylim = c(-10, 10)),
  list(y = y_neg_1,   label = "-1",     ylim = c(-10, 10)),
  list(y = y_neg_075, label = "-0.6",   ylim = c(-10, 10)),
  list(y = y_neg_025, label = "-0.25",  ylim = c(-10, 10)),
  list(y = y_squared, label = "0",      ylim = c(-10, 10))
)

plots <- lapply(plot_data, function(d) {
  ggplot(data.frame(x = x, y = d$y), aes(x, y)) +
    geom_point(color = "grey", shape = ".", size = 2) +
    annotate(
      "text", x = 0, y = Inf,
      label = paste0("R[XY] == ", d$label),
      parse = TRUE, vjust = 1.5
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-10, 10), limits = c(-10, 10)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(-10, 10)) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = d$ylim) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_bw() 
})

wrap_plots(plots, nrow = 2, ncol = 4)
```

## Correlation Test

If two numeric variables $X$ and $Y$ have no linear relationship, the sample correlation $R_{XY}$ will be close to zero. Given a sample correlation calculated from a sample of size $n$, we can test whether the true correlation is zero or not. Let $\rho_{XY}$ be the true correlation between $X$ and $Y$.

### Hypotheses

The null hypothesis is $H_0$: $\rho_{XY} = 0$, and the alternative hypothesis is one of the following three kinds.

- $H_1$: $\rho_{XY} > 0$ (right-sided test)

- $H_1$: $\rho_{XY} < 0$ (left-sided test)

- $H_1$: $\rho_{XY} \ne 0$ (two-sided test)

### Test Statistic

The test statistic is given by

$$
T = \frac{R_{XY} - 0}{ \texttt{SE} }
$$

which is called a **T statistic** (for testing correlation). The denominator $\texttt{SE}$ is the **standard error** which quantifies the uncertainty of sample correlation $R_{XY}$, and it is given by

$$
\texttt{SE} = \sqrt{ \frac{1 - (R_{XY})^2}{ n - 2 } } \, . 
$$

Assuming $H_0$: $\rho_{XY} = 0$ is true, the null distribution of $T$ is the T distribution with $\nu$ degrees of freedom, $T \sim \mathcal{T}(\nu)$ where $\nu = n - 2$.

### P-value

Given $T = \texttt{t}$, the calculation of p-value depends on the direction of $H_1$ as follows:

- [Right-sided test]{.underline}: p = $1 - \texttt{pt}(\texttt{t}, \nu)$
- [Left-sided test]{.underline}: p = $\texttt{pt}(\texttt{t}, \nu)$
- [Two-sided test]{.underline}: p = $2 * \texttt{pt}(\texttt{t}, \nu)$ if $\texttt{t} < 0$ or p = $2 * (1 - \texttt{pt}(\texttt{t}, \nu))$ if $\texttt{t} > 0$


If p-value is less than a fixed significance level of $\alpha$, we conclude $H_1$. Otherwise, we conclude $H_0$. The universal definition of p-value is the probability of observing the currently observed test statistic or stronger evidence for $H_1$ under the assumption of $H_0$. To this end, if p-value is small, it is evidence against $H_0$ and supports $H_1$.

#### Example

For the purpose of demonstration, let $X$ be the semester units and $Y$ be the study hours per week in the population of college students. The parameter of interest is $\rho_{XY}$, the population correlation between $X$ and $Y$, and we calculated a sample correlation of $R_{XY} = 0.196$ in a sample of size $n = 110$. We can perform the right-sided correlation test, 

- $H_0$: $\rho_{XY} = 0$ 

- $H_1$: $\rho_{XY} > 0$

```{r}
#| label: hand-calc-corr
( r <- cor( hours ~ units, data = studyhours ) ) ### sample correlation
( n <- nrow(studyhours) ) ### sample size (number of rows in the data)
( se <- sqrt( (1 - r^2) / (n - 2) ) ) ### standard error
( t <- ( r - 0 ) / se ) ### T statistic
( p <- ( 1 - pt(t, n - 2) ) ) ### p-value
```

Even though we observed a weak positive correlation (@tbl-cor), at a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$, the sample (110 college students) strong evidence against the null in favor of the alternative that the true correlation is greater than 0 and the semester units and study hours have a positive linear relationship (T = 2.075, DF = 108, and p = 0.020, $\alpha = 0.05$).

### Using $\texttt{cor.test}$ Function in R

The $\texttt{cor.test}$ function is useful for the correlation test.

- The first argument is $\texttt{y} \sim \texttt{x}$ where $\texttt{x}$ and $\texttt{y}$ are numeric variables.

- $\texttt{data}$ is the data frame name.

- $\texttt{alternative}$ is the direction of alternative hypothesis. Specify $\texttt{"greater"}$ for a right-sided test, $\texttt{"less"}$ for a left-sided test, or $\texttt{"two.sided"}$ for a two-sided test.

```{r}
#| label: cor-test-study
cor.test( hours ~ units, data = studyhours, alternative = "greater")
```

We can also extra a confidence interval:

```{r}
#| label: cor-ci-study
cor.test( hours ~ units, data = studyhours, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int
```

How was the confidence interval constructed?




Interpret the confidence interval in context. 




## Case Study 3: Vietnam War Draft

During the Vietnam War (1955-1975), the U.S. Selective Service drafted about 2.2 million men between 1964 and 1973. The U.S. Selective Service randomly matched birth dates and lottery numbers, and men who had a lottery number of 195 or below should be on reserve. The question of interest is whether the lottery was truly random or not. Let us take a look at the dataset $\texttt{draft1969.csv}$.

```{r}
#| label: read-draft
draft <- read_csv("data/draft1969.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) ### read data
head(draft, 5) ### first 5 lines
tail(draft, 5) ### last 5 lines
```

The column $\texttt{DateNumeric}$ is the numeric birth date (e.g., 1 to 366 for January 1 to December 31), and the column $\texttt{Lottery}$ is the randomly matched lottery number (1 to 366). For example, healthy men who were born on January 1 were not drafted ($\texttt{Lottery} = 305$) and healthy men who were born on December 31 were drafted ($\texttt{Lottery} = 100$). To investigate whether the lottery was fair (purely random) or not, the correlation test can be applied where $X$ and $Y$ denote the numeric birth date and lottery number, respectively

$H_0$: $\rho_{XY} = 0$ 


$H_1$: $\rho_{XY} \ne 0$ 



```{r}
#| label: draft-scatter
gf_point( Lottery ~ DateNumeric, data = draft,
      xlab = "Numeric birth date",
      ylab = "Lottery number",
      title = "Vietnam War Draft (Dec. 1, 1969)" ) |> 
  gf_lm()

cor(Lottery ~ DateNumeric, data = draft)
```

Let us conduct the correlation test (two-sided) using the $\texttt{cor.test}$ function.

```{r}
#| label: cor-test-draft
cor.test( Lottery ~ DateNumeric, data = draft, alternative = "two.sided" )
```

Using $\alpha = 0.05$ interpret the results of the test in context. Is the draft "fair"?











## Case Study 4: Cigarette Consumption and Price in the United States {#sec-cig}

The dataset $\texttt{cigarettes.csv}$ is state-level data (46 states) aggregated in 1992. It includes the following columns.

- $\texttt{packs}$: annual average number of cigarette packs consumed per person older than 16

- $\texttt{price}$: average price of one pack of cigarettes

**Note:** Each row is not a person. It is the estimated average per person in each state.

The objective of data analysis is to test whether the expected cigarette consumption is lower when the price is higher or not. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the explanatory variable ($\texttt{price}$) and response variable ($\texttt{packs}$), and let $\rho_{XY}$ be the true correlation (parameter to be tested). Given the objective, the null hypothesis is 

- $H_0$: $\rho_{XY} = 0$

- $H_1$: $\rho_{XY} < 0$ (left-sided test). 


Below are the scatterplot and correlation test.
```{r}
#| label: read-cig
cig <- read_csv("data/cigarettes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(cig, 5)
tail(cig, 5)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-cig
gf_point( packs ~ price, data = cig,
      xlab = "Average price (dollars per pack)",
      ylab = "Aerage consumption (packs per person)",
      title = "Cigarette Price and Consumption by State" ) |> 
  gf_lm()
```

```{r}
#| label: cor-cig
cor.test( packs ~ price, data = cig, alternative = "less" )
```

Using $\alpha = 0.05$ interpret the results of the test in context. How does cost affect smoking?







## Correlation vs. Causation

Let $X$ be an explanatory variable and $Y$ be a response variable. We say that $X$ and $Y$ have a **causal relationship** when the change of $X$ results in the change of $Y$. The sample correlation quantifies the linear relationship between $X$ and $Y$, and it does not verify whether the relationship is causal or not. In other words, [correlation does not imply causation]{.underline}.

When researchers control the value $X$ and randomly assign it to cases to then measure its effect on $Y$, it is called an **experimental study**. Otherwise, (i.e., researchers observe $X$ and $Y$ without controlling/randomly assigning $X$), it is called an **observational study**. An experimental study can verify a causal relationship if experimenters can randomly assign $X$ to each case and do it carefully. An observational study cannot verify a causal relationship, and sometimes it results in a significant correlation between $X$ and $Y$ even when they are not causally related.

Does long hair cause long lifetime of human? Here is a hypothetical experiment. Suppose an experimenter samples people from the population and randomly assigns Group 1 or 2. Group 1 is forced to keep their hair short, Group 2 is forced to keep their hair long, and the experimenter records their lifetime. Disregarding the fact that this hypothetical experiment is unrealistic (taking about 100 years) and unethical (forcing human subjects), the experimenter probably will not obtain evidence for the causal relationship between hair length and lifetime.

In an observational study, however, we may observe a positive correlation between hair length and lifetime. It is because women have longer hair than men on average, and the expected lifetime of women is longer than of men. The correlation between the explanatory variable (hair length) and the response variable (lifetime) exists through the third variable (sex). When a third variable is related to both explanatory variable and response variable, the third variable is called a **confounding variable** or **confounder**. In an observational study, we may observe a correlation between the explanatory variable and the response variable because of a confounding variable. Therefore, it is dangerous to claim a causal relationship based on the correlation observed in an observational study.

In this regard, we shall carefully state the conclusion of Case Study 4 (@sec-cig). We observed a statistically meaningful correlation between cigarette price and consumption, but it is [not]{.underline} evidence for the causation that lower cigarette price will reduce cigarette consumption (even if it is true). In order to obtain evidence for the causal relationship, we shall manipulate the cigarette price of each state and see if it affects the cigarette consumption. Can any researcher manipulate the cigarette price of each state in the United States? As such, conducting an experiment is challenging or sometimes nearly impossible in practice.

The following case study is another observational study, and demonstrates the caveat of an observational study.

## Case Study 5: Speed Limit and Car Accident Rate

The top three causes of car accidents are known to be distracted driving, speeding, and driving under influence. This analysis focuses on speeding, specifically the relationship between speed limit and accident rate on highways in Minnesota. The dataset $\texttt{highway.csv}$ is a sample of 39 highway sections in Minnesota, and the data were collected in 1973. The column $\texttt{rate}$ is the accident rate per million vehicle miles in each highway section (response variable), and the column $\texttt{slim}$ is the speed limit of the highway section (explanatory variable). The objective is to test at a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$

- $H_0$: $\rho_{XY} = 0$



- $H_1$: $\rho_{XY} > 0$ 



```{r}
#| label: read-highway
highway <- read_csv( "data/highway.csv", show_col_types =  )
head( highway, 5 )
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-highway
gf_point( rate ~ slim, data = highway,
      title = "Minnesota Highways in 1973",
      xlab = "Speed limit (mph)",
      ylab = "Accident rate (per million vehicle miles)" ) |> 
  gf_lm()
```


```{r}
#| label: cor-highway
cor.test( rate ~ slim, data = highway, alternative = "greater" )
```

Interpret the p-value.



Evaluate the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis.


Can you claim that the data suggest that low speed limit causes more accidents? 




Let us analyze pairwise correlations among other variables in the data: 

```{r}
#| label: cor-matrix
highway |> 
  select(rate, slim, shld, sigs1, acpt) |> 
  cor()
```

Potential confounding variables (moderately to strongly correlated with $\texttt{rate}$ and $\texttt{slim}$) are:

- $\texttt{shld}$: the width of highway shoulder in feet (negatively correlated with $\texttt{rate}$ and positively correlated with $\texttt{slim}$)

- $\texttt{sigs1}$: the adjusted number of signals per mile (positively correlated with $\texttt{rate}$ and negatively correlated with $\texttt{slim}$)

- $\texttt{acpt}$: the number of access points (traffic merging points) per mile (positively correlated with $\texttt{rate}$ and negatively correlated with $\texttt{slim}$)

Perhaps, the above potential confounding variables (risk factors) have causal relationships with accidents ($\texttt{rate}$) while the speed limit ($\texttt{slim}$) was lowered due to the risk factors. The take-home message is that it is very difficult to verify the causal relationship with an observational study, and the sample correlation may results in the opposite direction of the expected direction.

#### Problem 1 
Suppose we have four hypothetical samples as shown below.

```{r}
#| label: cor-samples
#| echo: false
par( mfrow=c(1,4) )

n = 30

set.seed(123)
x = runif( n, 0, 1 )
y = 1 * x + rnorm( n, 0, 0.3 )
plot( x, y, axes=FALSE, xlab="", ylab="", main="Sample 1" )
axis( 1, seq( -100, 100, 200 ) )
axis( 2, seq( -100, 100, 200 ) )
#cor( x, y )

set.seed(2)
x = runif( n, 0, 1 )
y = x + rnorm( n, 0, 0.05 )
plot( x, y, axes=FALSE, xlab="", ylab="", main="Sample 2" )
axis( 1, seq( -100, 100, 200 ) )
axis( 2, seq( -100, 100, 200 ) )
#cor( x, y )

set.seed(3)
x = runif( n, -1, 1 )
y = 2 * x^2 + rnorm( n, 0, 0.2 )
plot( x, y, axes=FALSE, xlab="", ylab="", main="Sample 3" )
axis( 1, seq( -100, 100, 200 ) )
axis( 2, seq( -100, 100, 200 ) )
#cor( x, y )

set.seed(4)
x = runif( n, 0, 1 )
y = -1 * x + rnorm( n, 0, 0.05 )
plot( x, y, axes=FALSE, xlab="", ylab="", main="Sample 4" )
axis( 1, seq( -100, 100, 200 ) )
axis( 2, seq( -100, 100, 200 ) )
#cor( x, y )

```

a. Multiple-choice: Which sample results in a sample correlation closest to +1?

\(A\) Sample 1; (B) Sample 2; (C) Sample 3; (D) Sample 4

b. Multiple-choice: Which sample results in a sample correlation closest to –1?

\(A\) Sample 1; (B) Sample 2; (C) Sample 3; (D) Sample 4

c. Multiple-choice: Which sample results in a sample correlation closest to 0?

\(A\) Sample 1; (B) Sample 2; (C) Sample 3; (D) Sample 4

#### Problem 2 
Suppose we have five hypothetical samples as follows:

- Sample 1: $R_{XY} = 0.9$ and $n = 5$

- Sample 2: $R_{XY} = 0.5$ and $n = 50$

- Sample 3: $R_{XY} = 0.1$ and $n = 5000$

- Sample 4: $R_{XY} = -0.5$ and $n = 50$

- Sample 5: $R_{XY} = -0.9$ and $n = 5$

a. Calculate T statistic for Sample 1.

b. Which sample provides the strongest evidence for a positive linear relationship between $X$ and $Y$?

\(A\) Sample 1; (B) Sample 2; (C) Sample 3; (D) Sample 4; (E) Sample 5

c. Which sample provides the strongest evidence for a negative linear relationship between $X$ and $Y$?

\(A\) Sample 1; (B) Sample 2; (C) Sample 3; (D) Sample 4; (E) Sample 5

#### Problem 3 
The dataset $\texttt{Guber99.csv}$ provides information about expenditures of public elementary and secondary schools and SAT scores in the 50 states for the academic year of 1994-95. It is a state-level data, and each row is the average measure of each state. The column $\texttt{verbal}$ is the average SAT verbal score in each state, $\texttt{math}$ is the average SAT math score in each state, $\texttt{perctakers}$ is the percent of eligible students who took SAT in each state, and $\texttt{expendpp}$ is the annual expenditure in public elementary and secondary schools (in \$1,000 per student). The researchers want to know whether the state-average SAT math score can be explained by expenditures of public elementary and secondary schools. It is believed that public education spending should help students' math skills measured by the SAT math score. Answer the following questions.

a. Multiple-choice: Which column represents the explanatory variable of interest?

\(A\) $\texttt{verbal}$; (B) $\texttt{math}$; (C) $\texttt{perctakers}$; (D) $\texttt{expendpp}$

b. Multiple-choice: Which column represents the response variable of interest?

\(A\) $\texttt{verbal}$; (B) $\texttt{math}$; (C) $\texttt{perctakers}$; (D) $\texttt{expendpp}$

c. Multiple-choice: Let $X$ and $Y$ denote the explanatory variable and response variable of interest, respectively. Which of the following represents the null hypothesis for the correlation test?

\(A\) $\rho_{XY} = 0$, (B) $\rho_{XY} > 0$, (C) $\rho_{XY} < 0$, (D) $\rho_{XY} \ne 0$

d. Multiple-choice: Which of the following represents the alternative hypothesis for the correlation test?

\(A\) $\rho_{XY} = 0$, (B) $\rho_{XY} > 0$, (C) $\rho_{XY} < 0$, (D) $\rho_{XY} \ne 0$

e. Multiple-choice: Choose the best description about this study.

\(A\) It is an experimental study which can show the linear relationship (correlation) between $X$ and $Y$.

\(B\) It is an experimental study which can show the causal relationship between $X$ and $Y$.

\(C\) It is an observational study which can show the linear relationship (correlation) between $X$ and $Y$.

\(D\) It is an observational study which can show the causal relationship between $X$ and $Y$.

\(E\) It can be either study depending on how we analyze the data.

f. Report the p-value for the correlation test.

g. State the conclusion in the context at a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$. (Use the concluding statements in the case studies as a template.)

h. Provide the scatterplot of $\texttt{expendpp}$ (x-axis) and $\texttt{perctakers}$ (y-axis). Calculate their sample correlation.

i. Provide the scatterplot of $\texttt{perctakers}$ (x-axis) and $\texttt{math}$ (y-axis).Calculate their sample correlation.

j. Provide the scatterplot of $\texttt{expendpp}$ (x-axis) and $\texttt{math}$ (y-axis). Calculate their sample correlation.

k. If you conducted the correlation test correctly in the previous part, you would not find evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis. Instead, the observed direction of the linear relationship between $X$ and $Y$ is the opposite of the alternative hypothesis. Explain this weird result by summarizing your findings in the previous parts. (You are recommended to use the following key words: observational study, explanatory variable, response variable, confounding variable, correlation, causation.)
